newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Toyota eyes 25 pct of S.Africa market in 97.
newsitem.headline: Toyota eyes 25 pct of S.Africa market in 97.

text.p: Toyota South Africa Ltd said on Thursday it aimed to increase its share of the country's new car sales to at least 25 percent in 1997, rising to 30 percent over the next four to five years.

The group, in which Japan's Toyota Motor Corp bought a 28.7 percent stake in October, last year saw its cut of the local market shrink to just below 24 percent last year from 24.7 percent in 1995, buffetted by intense competition.

"We have set a target for ourselves that we have to achieve a market share of at least 25 percent this year and in the coming year...We will try our hardest to achieve 30 percent over the next four to five years," Bert Wessels, the chief executive officer, told reporters.
He said production of around 110,000 units was needed to meet these targets, rising to 140,000 for a 30 percent slice.
The group was also keen to expand exports into Africa from around 2,500 in 12 countries last year to 6,000 in a few years time, adding states including Senegal and Ghana to the client list.

Increased production would require a hefty capital injection and Wessels said the firm planned to pump some 1.275 billion rand -- to be funded out of retained profits -- into new facilities, tooling and training in the period 1997 to 2000.
"We have to do this to meet competition...but we are not breaking out into cold sweats on whether we can fund these requirements," Wessels said.
Toyota last week released year results showing a four percent drop in earnings to 196.2 million rand.

Wessels said the group aimed to cut costs by on average three percent a year over the next seven years, a move necessary to withstand heightened foreign competition as South Africa's vehicle tariffs were reduced.
"As time goes on with the lowering of duties it is inevitable that we will have to bring prices down in real terms."

However, Wessels said Toyota's prices may in 1997 rise by close to or even exceed inflation slightly after it went "overboard" last year when prices were upped by a slim 2.5 percent compared with average inflation of 7.4 percent.

On prospects for the motor industry in South Africa this year, vehicle marketing head Johan van Zyl said new car sales would expand this year but come off the heady levels of around 14 percent seen in the first two months of this year.

"We do not see the current high level of growth in passenger sales being sustained through the year but rather a situation where the market stabilises to produce sales very much in line or marginally above those achieved in 1996," van Zyl said.
New car sales grew by just over 5.6 percent in 1996 compared with 1995.
The National Association of Automobile Manufacturers of South Africa in January said it expected a slight drop in car sales this year as high interest rates cut into consumers' disposable income.
